title: Ordinances
lead: Conceived from the ==GoI Act, 1935==; only ==India, Pakistan and Bangladesh== permit ordinance-making in parliamentary democracies. Recently the SC's strength was raised to ==37 via an Ordinance== right before the summer vacation — raising questions on urgency and necessity.
intro: For in the quiet expansion of ordinance-making lies the loud warning of democratic decay. The future of India's constitutional order depends on restoring law-making to the chamber of elected debate, not the corridors of executive decree.

items: Only when ==either House is not in session==
Only on the respective ==ordinary legislative powers== of Parliament / State Legislatures
Must be passed ==within the first 6 weeks== of the House reassembling
President/Governor can ==return or reject== Central/State Ordinances
Governor ==can't promulgate== on something that should have been ==reserved for the President==

items.title: Rationale
bullets: An ==exceptional tool==, not a routine one

items.title: Data
bullets: Peaks: ==1990–99 (196)== and ==1970–79 (133)== — political instability and coalitions
States re-promulgate heavily — ==Kerala reissued 140 of 144 ordinances in 2021==

items.title: Post-Lapse Prognosis
bullets: Actions under the ordinance may remain valid — ==doctrine of past operation==
Rights conferred or taken away ==may be lost== unless expressly saved or re-enacted

items: Six recurring problems: ==misuse for political expediency, re-promulgation, lack of scrutiny, no cap, post-lapse impact, bypassing committees==.
==Jurisprudence gaps==: mixed signals, evolving review, need for stronger standards, and a persistent ==implementation gap==.

head: Case
Holding
rows: [[A.K. Roy v. UoI (1982)]]
==Urgency is essential== — ordinances are not a substitute for regular lawmaking.
[[D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987)]]
Re-promulgation is a ==‘fraud on the Constitution’==.
[[Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (2017)]]
Ordinance ==must be laid before the legislature==; re-promulgation unconstitutional.

sections.title: Good Use of the Ordinance Route

head: Example
Why justified
rows: ==Epidemic Diseases (Amendment) Ordinance, 2020==
Sudden COVID emergency — prohibited violence against healthcare personnel; later enacted by Parliament.
IBC amendment during COVID-19, 2020
Temporary insolvency changes as ==emergency economic relief==.
IIITDM Kancheepuram Ordinance, 2011
Urgent statutory recognition so graduating students could lawfully receive degrees — a ==classic temporary legal gap==.
Criminal Law Amendment Ordinance, 2013
Post-2012 Delhi gang rape — extraordinary public-safety concern; but a Bill and committee process were already underway, so a ==qualified== example.

head: Example
Why it represents misuse
rows: Repeated Bihar Ordinances — [[Krishna Kumar Singh]]
Repeated re-promulgation on takeover of Sanskrit schools ==without legislative approval==.
==Land Acquisition Amendment Ordinances, 2014–15==
Re-promulgated thrice while replacement legislation was under parliamentary examination.
Enemy Property Amendment Ordinances, 2016
Same policy continued through successive Ordinances while legislation stayed pending.
==Tribunals Reforms Ordinance, 2021==
Structural reform via ordinance — avoiding deliberative scrutiny, not a sudden emergency.
Bank nationalisation Ordinance, 1969
Scale and permanence raised the question of using urgency to ==avoid prior debate==.
Ordinances issued right after a session ends
Waiting for adjournment then promulgating on a ==foreseeable matter== makes urgency doubtful.
Ordinances reproducing stalled Bills
==Political difficulty is not the ‘necessity’== contemplated by Art 123.

blocks.text: An Ordinance should bridge a legislative vacuum, not manufacture parliamentary consent.
